title: CERV-2026-DAPHNE: EU Grants to Prevent and Combat Gender-Based Violence and Violence Against Children
summary: The European Union has opened the CERV-2026-DAPHNE Call for Proposals , a major funding opportunity under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) Programme designed to support organisations working to prevent and combat gender-based violence and violence against children. With an estimated €21 million total budget , the call will support projects addressing victim protection and support, prevention of gender-based violence, child protection systems, implementation of European legal frameworks, and financial and capacity-building support for grassroots civil society organisations. What Is the CERV-2026-DAPHNE Call? The CERV-2026-DAPHNE call is part of the European Union s broader effort to protect fundamental rights, promote equality and strengthen societies ability to prevent and respond to violence. The Daphne strand of CERV specifically focuses on combating violence, including gender-based violence and violence against children. The 2026 call seeks projects that address different forms of violence through prevention, victim and survivor support, stronger child-protection systems, policy implementation and support to civil society. The European Commission highlights that gender-based violence remains closely connected to gender inequality and can have significant social, human and economic consequences. The 2026 call also places particular emphasis on emerging forms of violence, including online and technology-facilitated violence. The call is aligned with several EU policy frameworks, including the EU Gender Equality Strategy 2026–2030, the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child, the Istanbul Convention and the EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence. Five Funding Priorities Under CERV-2026-DAPHNE Applicants should carefully select the priority that most closely matches their organisation s expertise and proposed project because one proposal can address only one of the five topics . 1. Supporting Intermediary Organisations and Grassroots Civil Society Organisations Topic: CERV-2026-DAPHNE-REGRANTING The first priority focuses on organisations that can act as intermediaries and provide financial support and capacity building to smaller grassroots civil society organisations working on gender-based violence and/or violence against children. The objective is not simply to fund one organisation s activities. Instead, successful intermediary organisations will be expected to create mechanisms through which funding and capacity-building support can reach smaller and grassroots organisations. Particular attention is given to organisations operating in: Remote areas Rural communities Underserved communities Areas where grassroots organisations have limited access to funding Settings where smaller civil society organisations have limited institutional capacity Activities can address areas such as: Domestic violence Sexual violence Gender-based cyberviolence Violence against children Victim protection Victim-centred services Access to justice Medical and psychological support Capacity building Organisational development Community-level prevention For this priority, applicants must demonstrate recent experience in CSO capacity building and experience in awarding and managing grants in the relevant fields. The call requires at least three years of recent proven experience in implementing CSO capacity-building activities related to gender-based violence and/or violence against children. Funding under Priority 1 Minimum requested grant: €1 million Maximum requested grant: €2.5 million Project duration: 36 months Regranting: Mandatory Application: Single applicant or consortium Geographical scope: National or transnational Click HERE to read more and apply. 2. Protecting and Supporting Victims and Survivors of Gender-Based Violence Topic: CERV-2026-DAPHNE-PROTECTION The second priority focuses on improving protection and support for victims and survivors of gender-based violence. Projects can seek to strengthen services that help victims and survivors access appropriate support, protection and justice. Potential areas of work include: Victim support services Survivor-centred approaches Domestic violence services Sexual violence support Access to justice Psychological and psychosocial support Medical support Protection mechanisms Trauma-informed services Support for children affected by domestic violence Services for people facing multiple or intersecting forms of discrimination The call encourages applicants to develop integrated approaches rather than isolated interventions. Funding under Priority 2 Grant range: €200,000–€600,000 Duration: 12–24 months Application: Consortium of at least two applicants Scope: National or transnational Public authority involvement: Recommended Click HERE to read more and apply. 3. Preventing Gender-Based Violence Topic: CERV-2026-DAPHNE-PREVENTION The third priority focuses on preventing gender-based violence before it occurs and addressing the social, cultural and structural factors that contribute to violence. Projects under this priority can focus on prevention strategies, awareness, education, behavioural change, community engagement, research, communication and other approaches that contribute to reducing gender-based violence. Potential areas may include: Prevention campaigns Awareness-raising Community education Gender equality initiatives Prevention of domestic violence Prevention of sexual violence Prevention of online gender-based violence Addressing harmful social norms Training professionals Improving prevention systems Community-based interventions Research and evidence generation Digital safety and prevention The call places significant importance on integrating gender and non-discrimination considerations into project design. Funding under Priority 3 Grant range: €200,000–€600,000 Duration: 12–24 months Application: Consortium of at least two applicants Scope: National or transnational Public authority involvement: Recommended Click HERE to read more and apply. 4. Supporting the EU Directive on Violence Against Women Topic: CERV-2026-DAPHNE-CONVENTION-DIR The fourth priority is specifically focused on supporting implementation of the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence , commonly known as the Istanbul Convention , as well as the EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence. This priority is particularly relevant for organisations working on: Policy reform Legislative implementation Public administration Legal systems Gender-based violence policy Domestic violence prevention Victim protection Training of relevant professionals Awareness raising Monitoring and evaluation Research Implementation of legislation Institutional capacity building Important eligibility distinction For Priority 4, the lead applicant must be a public authority at national, regional or local level . Co-applicants can include: Public entities Private non-profit organisations Private for-profit organisations International organisations Funding under Priority 4 Grant range: €200,000–€600,000 Duration: 12–24 months Application: Single applicant or consortium Lead applicant: Public authority Scope: National or transnational Click HERE to read more and apply. 5. Strengthening Integrated Child Protection Systems Topic: CERV-2026-DAPHNE-CHILDREN The fifth priority focuses on strengthening integrated systems for protecting children from violence. The European Commission promotes a coordinated, child-centred approach in which different sectors and institutions work together rather than operating separately. Projects may address: Child protection systems Prevention of violence against children Child-centred services Cross-sectoral collaboration Child safeguarding Child participation Prevention of child sexual abuse Prevention of bullying and cyberbullying Protection against domestic violence Mental health and psychosocial support Referral systems Early identification and reporting Monitoring and evaluation Coordination between government agencies and civil society Protection of children in vulnerable situations The call recognises that violence against children can occur both offline and online and can include physical or mental violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and sexual abuse. Funding under Priority 5 Grant range: €200,000–€600,000 Duration: 12–24 months Application: Consortium of at least two applicants Scope: National or transnational Public authority involvement: Mandatory Organisations whose projects involve children must also have an appropriate child protection policy covering the required safeguarding areas. Click HERE to read more and apply. Who Can Apply? This is an important point: CERV-2026-DAPHNE is not an individual grant opportunity. It is designed primarily for organisations and institutions , rather than individuals applying in their personal capacity. Eligible applicants generally need to be legal entities , including public or private bodies, established in an eligible country. International organisations can also participate, and the call contains specific rules for entities without separate legal personality and other types of participants. For priorities 2, 3 and 5, applications must generally be submitted by a consortium of at least two eligible applicants . For Priority 1 and Priority 4, applications can be submitted either by a single applicant or by a consortium, subject to the specific requirements of the priority. National or International Projects Projects under all five priorities can be either: National , or Transnational However, the consortium requirements differ by priority. For organisations considering a transnational application, the partnership should provide clear added value rather than simply satisfying a formal requirement. The European Commission specifically expects partnerships to demonstrate complementary expertise and an appropriate distribution of responsibilities and resources. Key Areas That Could Make a Strong Proposal A competitive application should go beyond describing the problem. A strong proposal should clearly demonstrate: A clearly defined problem Evidence-based needs assessment A clearly identified target population A strong connection to one of the five priorities A realistic intervention model Strong organisational capacity Appropriate partners Clear roles and responsibilities Measurable outputs and outcomes A credible monitoring and evaluation system A realistic budget A strong sustainability plan A dissemination and communication strategy Alignment with EU values and policy priorities The proposal should also demonstrate how its results can continue to generate impact beyond the period of EU funding. This is particularly important because Impact accounts for 20 of the 100 available evaluation points . Important Compliance Requirements Applicants should also pay close attention to compliance. Organisations must have sufficient financial and operational capacity to implement the project. The European Commission may assess: Financial statements Revenue Deficits Dependence on EU funding Previous project experience Staff qualifications Technical resources Organisational capacity Organisations can also be excluded for serious issues such as certain financial, legal, tax, social-security, professional misconduct, fraud, corruption or other exclusion circumstances. Application Process Applications must be submitted electronically through the EU Funding Tenders Portal . Paper applications are not accepted. Applicants should: Identify the most appropriate CERV-2026-DAPHNE priority. Carefully review the eligibility requirements. Confirm that the organisation and proposed partners are eligible. Register the relevant entities in the Participant Register. Develop the project concept. Identify appropriate partners where a consortium is required. Prepare the needs assessment. Develop the methodology and work plan. Establish measurable objectives and indicators. Prepare the detailed budget. Prepare CVs and supporting organisational documents. Complete the application forms through the Submission System. Upload the required supporting documents. Review the proposal against the evaluation criteria. Submit before the deadline. The Commission states that beneficiaries and affiliated entities must be registered in the Participant Register before submitting the proposal and will undergo legal-entity validation. Who Should Consider Applying? This opportunity may be particularly relevant for eligible organisations such as: Non-profit civil society organisations NGOs Women s rights organisations Organisations working on gender equality Organisations working on gender-based violence Organisations supporting survivors Child protection organisations Organisations working on violence prevention Public authorities Local and regional authorities Research and policy organisations International organisations Organisations with expertise in child protection Organisations working on digital violence and online safety Organisations providing psychosocial or victim support Organisations with experience in advocacy and policy implementation However, eligibility depends on the specific priority , the applicant s legal status, country of establishment, consortium requirements and other conditions. Important Advice Before Applying Applicants should not begin by writing the proposal . The stronger approach is to first determine which of the five priorities is the best fit. For example: An organisation funding and strengthening grassroots CSOs may consider Priority 1 . A survivor-support organisation may consider Priority 2 . A prevention and awareness organisation may consider Priority 3 . A public authority working on implementation of relevant legislation may consider Priority 4 . A child protection organisation working on integrated systems may consider Priority 5 . The proposal should then be built around the selected priority rather than trying to make one project fit multiple priorities. The Commission explicitly states that each proposal must address only one of the five topics . Conclusion The CERV-2026-DAPHNE Call for Proposals represents a substantial European Union funding opportunity for organisations working to prevent and combat gender-based violence and violence against children. With an estimated €21 million available , the call provides funding across five major areas: grassroots civil society support through regranting, victim and survivor protection, prevention of gender-based violence, implementation of European frameworks on violence against women, and integrated child protection systems. title: Call for Research Proposals: Economic Opportunities for Women and Men — How Regulation and Fiscal Policy Shape Economic Opportunities in Latin America and the Caribbean
summary: The Gender and Diversity Lab (GDLab) , an initiative of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Group , has launched a new Call for Research Proposals on “Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy.” The call seeks research proposals that can generate rigorous, credible, and policy-relevant evidence on one of the most important questions facing economies in Latin America and the Caribbean: how government regulations, financial systems, fiscal policies, and labor-market reforms affect the economic opportunities available to women and men, and how public policy can help reduce gender differences in economic outcomes. Through this initiative, GDLab and the IDB s Institutions for Development Sector are looking to support research that goes beyond describing gender gaps. Instead, the call emphasizes causal research capable of determining whether particular policies, reforms, regulations, or interventions actually produce different outcomes for women and men. Researchers are encouraged to develop studies that can provide practical evidence for governments, private-sector organizations, and multilateral institutions seeking to design more effective policies and programs. The deadline for applications is September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon) . Key Details at a Glance Opportunity Details Organizer GDLab, an IDB Group initiative, in collaboration with the IDB s Institutions for Development Sector Opportunity Call for Research Proposals Research theme Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy Geographic focus Latin America and the Caribbean Eligible research countries One or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries Research approach Rigorous quantitative causal research Accepted methodologies Experimental, quasi-experimental, and structural models Qualitative research Considered only when supporting the quantitative analysis Funding Available under the funding categories specified in the official brochure Application platform Oxford Abstracts Deadline September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon) Research outputs External peer review; potential consideration for the IDB Working Paper Series; academic publication encouraged About the Research Call Gender differences in economic opportunities can emerge from many aspects of economic and institutional systems. Regulations can influence whether women and men can enter particular occupations, establish businesses, access financial services, participate in the labor market, or benefit equally from economic reforms. Similarly, fiscal policy can affect households, workers, businesses, and entrepreneurs differently depending on gender, income, employment status, family responsibilities, and access to economic resources. The new GDLab call is designed to support research that investigates these relationships systematically. Rather than simply asking whether a gender gap exists, researchers are expected to examine questions such as: What causes differences in economic opportunities between women and men? Which regulations create or reduce barriers to women s economic participation? Do financial policies affect women and men differently? How do fiscal reforms influence women s and men s labor-market outcomes? What happens when governments introduce a particular policy or regulatory reform? Which interventions are effective at reducing gender disparities? Are some policies more effective for certain groups of women or men? What policy instruments can governments use to expand economic opportunities? How can governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations use evidence to design more effective interventions? The emphasis on causal research is particularly important because the organizers are seeking evidence that can help distinguish correlation from actual policy effects. Main Objective of the Call The central objective is to support rigorous causal research addressing two broad areas. 1. Understanding how reforms affect women and men differently The call seeks research examining how regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms affect economic opportunities for women and men. This could include studying whether a particular reform changes: Labor-force participation Employment Earnings Entrepreneurship Business creation Access to finance Business growth Occupational opportunities Formal employment Access to economic resources Productivity Economic mobility Other relevant measures of economic opportunity Researchers should be able to establish credible relationships between the policy or reform being studied and the resulting outcomes. 2. Identifying policies that can reduce gender differences The second major objective is to understand how policy instruments can improve economic opportunities and reduce differences between women and men . This moves the research from diagnosis toward solutions. The strongest studies may therefore demonstrate not only that a gender gap exists, but also identify which policy interventions can effectively address the gap and under what circumstances . What Topics Will the Research Call Prioritize? The call focuses broadly on the relationship between economic opportunity, gender, regulation, fiscal policy, financial systems, and labor-market policies . Researchers may investigate how different forms of government intervention influence women and men differently. Potential research areas can include the following. 1. Regulatory Reforms Regulations can have significant effects on people s ability to participate in economic activity. Research could examine how changes in regulations affect women and men in areas such as: Employment Entrepreneurship Business registration Business ownership Occupational access Labor-market participation Business operations Access to markets Formalization Economic activity A strong proposal could investigate whether a regulatory reform removes barriers to women s participation or unintentionally creates new constraints. 2. Financial Policies and Access to Finance Access to financial services is another important component of economic opportunity. Researchers could examine whether women and men experience different outcomes from: Credit policies Financial inclusion programs Lending reforms Access to business finance Financial regulations Credit guarantees Digital financial services Other financial policy instruments The research could investigate whether financial reforms improve women s ability to start, operate, or expand businesses and whether the effects differ from those experienced by men. 3. Fiscal Policy Fiscal policies can influence economic decisions and opportunities through taxation, government spending, transfers, subsidies, and other mechanisms. Researchers could examine whether fiscal reforms have different effects on women and men. Possible questions could include: Does a particular tax reform affect women and men differently? Do government transfers increase women s economic participation? Can fiscal incentives encourage women s entrepreneurship? Do public spending programs improve women s access to economic opportunities? How do fiscal policies interact with household responsibilities? Are certain fiscal instruments more effective at reducing gender disparities? The objective would be to produce evidence that can inform future fiscal-policy decisions. 4. Labor-Market Reforms Labor-market policies are directly connected to economic opportunity. Researchers could study the effects of reforms involving: Employment regulations Labor-market participation Working conditions Employment protections Formal employment Wages Hiring Occupational mobility Other labor-market outcomes The research should examine whether particular policies create different effects for women and men and whether reforms can reduce existing disparities. Why Causal Research Is Central to This Opportunity One of the most important requirements of this call is that proposals use rigorous quantitative methods capable of establishing causal relationships . This means that applicants should not simply present descriptive statistics showing that women and men have different economic outcomes. For example, a study showing that women earn less than men would demonstrate a gender difference, but by itself it would not establish what caused that difference . The call is interested in research that can answer stronger questions such as: What was the effect of a specific policy, regulation, or reform on women s economic outcomes compared with what would have happened without that intervention? This distinction makes the methodological component of the proposal extremely important. Methodologies That May Be Used The call specifically identifies several rigorous quantitative approaches. Experimental Designs Experimental research can be used when researchers can credibly introduce or evaluate an intervention and compare outcomes between relevant groups. For example, researchers could evaluate whether a particular policy intervention changes economic outcomes for women compared with an appropriate comparison group. Quasi-Experimental Designs Quasi-experimental methods can be particularly useful when researchers cannot randomly assign policies or interventions. Depending on the research question and available data, appropriate approaches could include methods designed to exploit: Policy changes Regulatory reforms Eligibility thresholds Geographic variation Timing differences Other institutional or policy changes The key requirement is that the chosen methodology must provide a credible strategy for identifying causal effects. Structural Models The call also allows the use of structural models . These approaches can be useful when researchers want to model economic behavior and simulate how alternative policies or reforms could affect outcomes. A structural approach may therefore allow researchers to examine not only the effect of an existing policy but potentially the implications of alternative policy scenarios. Role of Qualitative Research The call does not completely exclude qualitative research. However, qualitative components will be considered only to the extent that they support the implementation of the quantitative analysis . This means that a proposal centered primarily on qualitative interviews, focus groups, narratives, or descriptive case studies may not align well with the call s methodological expectations. A stronger approach would be to use qualitative information strategically to: Inform the design of the quantitative research Help understand the institutional context Support interpretation of quantitative findings Improve implementation of the research strategy Help explain mechanisms behind quantitative results The quantitative causal component should remain central. Geographic Scope: Latin America and the Caribbean A critical eligibility condition is the geographic focus of the research. Only proposals analyzing one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries will be considered. This means researchers should ensure that their proposed study has a clear connection to an eligible IDB borrowing member country. Applicants should therefore verify the IDB s official list of borrowing member countries before developing their proposal. The geographic requirement is important because the call is designed to generate evidence directly relevant to economic and policy challenges in the Latin America and Caribbean region . What Makes a Strong Proposal? Although the final proposal should follow the detailed requirements in the official brochure, the description of the call provides several clear indications of what the organizers are seeking. A competitive proposal should ideally demonstrate: 1. A clear research question The proposal should clearly explain what economic or policy question it intends to answer. 2. A strong gender dimension The research should meaningfully examine differences between women and men rather than simply mentioning gender as a secondary variable. 3. A clearly defined policy or reform The study should identify the relevant regulation, financial policy, fiscal reform, labor reform, or other policy instrument being evaluated. 4. A credible causal identification strategy The proposal needs to explain how the researchers will establish a causal relationship. 5. Appropriate quantitative data Applicants should demonstrate that the necessary data are available or realistically obtainable. 6. Policy relevance The research should have potential implications for real-world decision-making. 7. Actionable recommendations The call particularly encourages proposals that can generate recommendations for: Governments Private-sector organizations Multilateral organizations This makes policy applicability an important feature of a potentially competitive proposal. Potential Research Questions Applicants Could Explore The following examples illustrate the type of questions that could fit within the broad theme of the call. They are illustrative research directions , not an official list of required topics. Regulation How does a change in business registration regulation affect women s business creation? Do regulatory reforms affect female-owned businesses differently from male-owned businesses? Which regulatory barriers have the greatest effect on women s participation in formal economic activity? Finance Does improved access to formal credit increase women s entrepreneurship? Do financial reforms produce different business outcomes for women-owned and men-owned enterprises? What types of financial interventions most effectively reduce gender gaps in access to capital? Fiscal Policy How do changes in taxation affect women s labor-force participation? Do government transfers have different employment effects for women and men? Can targeted fiscal policies increase women s participation in economic activity? Labor Markets How do labor regulations influence women s formal employment? Do changes in employment protections affect women and men differently? Which labor-market reforms are most effective at reducing gender disparities? Again, the strongest proposal would need to translate such a question into a rigorous causal research design . Why This Research Matters Gender differences in economic opportunity are not simply individual-level issues. They can affect households, businesses, labor markets, productivity, income distribution, and broader economic development. When women face barriers to employment, entrepreneurship, finance, or economic participation, economies may fail to use a significant portion of their available human capital. Understanding which policies actually improve economic opportunities can therefore help governments allocate resources more effectively. This is particularly important because policies that appear gender-neutral on paper can sometimes have different effects on women and men . For example, a policy may technically apply equally to both groups but interact differently with: Household responsibilities Existing employment patterns Access to financial resources Business ownership Occupational segregation Labor-market participation Access to formal institutions Rigorous causal research can help policymakers identify these differences and design more effective interventions. Policy Impact Is a Major Component The call explicitly encourages research capable of generating actionable recommendations . This means the ultimate value of a successful study should extend beyond academic publication. Research findings could potentially help policymakers understand: Which policies work Which policies do not work For whom policies work How large the effects are Whether effects differ by gender What unintended consequences may exist How policies could be improved Whether an intervention can be scaled How limited public resources could be allocated more effectively The findings may also be relevant to private-sector organizations and multilateral institutions. Potential Benefits for Selected Researchers Selected studies will undergo external peer review , which can provide an additional layer of academic and methodological scrutiny. Selected research may also be considered for publication in the IDB Working Paper Series . In addition, the call encourages publication in academic journals. For researchers, this means the opportunity can potentially provide more than research funding. A successfully completed project could also contribute to: Academic research Policy evidence Regional economic policy discussions Gender-equality research Government decision-making Institutional research outputs Peer-reviewed publications Funding Available The call provides funding under categories specified by the organizers. Because the exact funding amounts and corresponding requirements are detailed in the official brochure, applicants should review the brochure carefully before preparing their budgets and submitting their proposals. Researchers should pay particular attention to: Available funding categories Maximum funding amounts Eligible expenses Research team requirements Proposal requirements Methodological expectations Application documentation Submission procedures Applicants should not rely solely on summaries of the call when preparing a submission. The official brochure should be treated as the authoritative source for the complete funding and eligibility conditions. Click HERE to learn more. How to Apply Applications must be submitted online through the Oxford Abstracts platform. The application process should be approached carefully because the proposal needs to demonstrate both substantive relevance and methodological rigor. Step 1: Review the Official Call Begin by reading the official brochure carefully. Pay particular attention to: Eligibility Research priorities Funding categories Proposal requirements Evaluation criteria Submission requirements Key dates Step 2: Select an Eligible Country Make sure the research analyzes one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries . Step 3: Define the Research Question Develop a precise question related to economic opportunities for women and men and the role of: Regulation Financial policy Fiscal policy Labor-market reform Other relevant policy instruments Step 4: Develop the Causal Strategy Explain exactly how the research will establish causal effects. The proposal should identify the appropriate quantitative methodology and demonstrate why it is suitable for the research question. Step 5: Demonstrate Data Feasibility Applicants should consider whether the necessary data exist and whether they can realistically be accessed and analyzed within the project s scope. Step 6: Explain Policy Relevance Clearly explain how the findings could inform policy decisions. Step 7: Develop Actionable Recommendations Where possible, demonstrate how the research could translate evidence into recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations. Step 8: Submit Through Oxford Abstracts The completed application must be submitted through the designated Oxford Abstracts application platform before the deadline. Application Deadline The deadline is: September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon). Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their proposals. Researchers should allow sufficient time to: Review eligibility requirements Develop the research question Finalize the methodology Verify data availability Prepare the research team information Develop the budget Review supporting documentation Complete the online application Resolve any technical issues with submission APPLY HERE Conclusion The GDLab Call for Research Proposals on Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy offers an important opportunity for researchers studying gender differences in economic participation and the effectiveness of public policy in Latin America and the Caribbean. The call is particularly suited to research teams capable of conducting rigorous quantitative causal analysis rather than purely descriptive or qualitative studies. Its emphasis on regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms creates a broad research space for investigators examining how policy decisions shape economic opportunities for women and men. A particularly strong application is likely to combine a well-defined policy question, a credible causal identification strategy, appropriate quantitative data, a clear gender dimension, and strong policy relevance . Researchers are also encouraged to ensure that their findings can translate into actionable recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral institutions. title: Monash University Fully Funded PhD Scholarships 2027: Up to Five AI and Society Research Scholarships With AUD 41,100 Annual Stipend
summary: Applications are now open for up to five PhD scholarships at Monash University in Australia for researchers interested in examining the human, social, ethical, political, cultural, economic and creative consequences of artificial intelligence. The Monash Arts “Shaping AI’s Future” PhD Scholarships are aimed particularly at researchers from the humanities, arts and social sciences who want to investigate how artificial intelligence is changing society and how people, institutions, cultures and political systems are simultaneously shaping the development and use of AI. Rather than concentrating primarily on the engineering or technical development of artificial intelligence, these PhD opportunities focus on the human dimensions of AI . Possible research areas include: AI governance and public policy Democracy and artificial intelligence Digital inequality Algorithmic discrimination Human-AI relationships Youth wellbeing and AI companionship AI and ageing Digital labour Automation and employment AI and creative industries Music and generative AI Screen aesthetics Misinformation and communication Public trust Cultural representation Ethics Surveillance Social cohesion Machine agency AI and knowledge production Artificial intelligence in education National security Geopolitics Environmental implications of AI Up to five scholarships will be awarded through the Faculty of Arts at Monash University. The scholarships provide a Research Living Allowance valued at AUD 41,100 per year at the 2027 full-time rate , paid as a tax-free stipend and indexed in accordance with applicable scholarship conditions. Additional allowances are available according to the relevant Research Training Program stipend scholarship rules. The opportunity is open to appropriately qualified domestic and international applicants. The announcement also states that successful international candidates will receive tuition support in addition to the stipend . Successful candidates will undertake their PhDs full-time and on campus at either the Clayton or Caulfield campus in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia . Applications close on: Wednesday, 30 September 2026 at 11:55 PM AEST. Successful candidates are expected to commence their PhD no later than 12 March 2027 . About the Monash University “Shaping AI’s Future” PhD Scholarships Artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, is developing and spreading through society at extraordinary speed. While much public discussion focuses on the technical capabilities of AI systems, Monash Arts argues that understanding artificial intelligence requires much more than engineering or computer science. AI also raises fundamental questions about: Human behaviour Social relationships Knowledge Politics Culture Communication Identity Ethics Employment Inequality Governance Security Creativity Public institutions The Faculty of Arts is therefore seeking doctoral researchers capable of investigating these broader dimensions of technological transformation. The programme emphasizes research from the Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences , commonly abbreviated as HASS . These disciplines provide theoretical, methodological and critical tools that can help explain how AI affects individuals and societies and how policy responses can be designed in ways that are effective, equitable and inclusive. Why Monash Arts Is Funding Research on the Human Side of AI AI is influencing increasingly large areas of everyday and institutional life. Among the issues identified by Monash Arts are questions surrounding AI s influence on: Social cohesion Knowledge production Education Culture Geopolitical competition National security Institutional trust Digital humanities Personal and intimate relationships Environmental sustainability Ethics Governance These developments create an urgent need for research capable of informing future decision-making. Monash Arts emphasizes that Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences researchers should play an active role in determining how AI is incorporated into society. The challenge is not simply to ask: “What can AI do?” Researchers also need to ask questions such as: How should AI be governed? Who benefits from AI? Who may be disadvantaged? How does AI change relationships between people and institutions? How might AI reinforce existing inequalities? What happens to work when automation expands? How does AI influence public trust and democracy? How should culture, creativity and authorship change in an AI-driven environment? How do people resist or reject AI? How should society think about responsibility and machine agency? These are precisely the kinds of questions the scholarship programme is designed to support. Number of PhD Scholarships Available Monash Arts is offering: Up to five PhD scholarships Selection will be competitive. The scholarships are intended for applicants capable of undertaking advanced interdisciplinary research addressing current or emerging challenges created by artificial intelligence and wider digital transformation. Applicants are not expected simply to replicate existing projects. The programme seeks researchers who can demonstrate: Intellectual curiosity Research potential Social awareness Strong academic preparation Understanding of the proposed field Ability to develop a credible doctoral project Scholarship Value Successful candidates will receive a: Research Living Allowance of AUD 41,100 per annum This is the stated: 2027 full-time rate The stipend is described as: Tax-free and is: Indexed Additional allowances may apply according to Monash University’s Research Training Program stipend scholarship conditions. Applicants should consult Monash University s current graduate research scholarship regulations for detailed rules governing payments, indexing and allowances. Tuition Support for International Candidates The programme announcement states that successful international candidates may receive: Full stipend Tuition support This makes the scholarships especially relevant to international applicants who would otherwise face substantial international doctoral tuition costs in Australia. Applicants should nevertheless review the formal scholarship conditions and final offer carefully because the specific tuition arrangements and scholarship components may depend on Monash graduate research rules. Scholarship Duration The opportunity is listed as a: 3.5-year fixed-term appointment This provides sufficient time for candidates to complete a structured doctoral research programme. The PhD must be undertaken: Full-time On campus It is therefore not advertised as an online or distance PhD. Where Will Successful Candidates Study? Successful applicants will be based at either: Monash University Clayton campus , or Monash University Caulfield campus Both campuses are located in the Melbourne metropolitan area in the state of Victoria, Australia. The exact campus will likely depend on the research project, academic unit and supervisory arrangements. About Monash University Monash University is a large internationally connected Australian university with multiple campuses and global partnerships. Successful PhD researchers will join a university environment with links across: Australia Asia Europe International research networks Monash Arts describes itself as a diverse faculty supporting: Disciplinary research Multidisciplinary research Interdisciplinary research Research within the Faculty operates at multiple levels, including: Individual experience Communities Societies Regions Nations International systems This broad intellectual environment is particularly relevant to AI research because artificial intelligence increasingly affects multiple areas of social life simultaneously. International Mobility Opportunities Successful candidates will have access to: International mobility grants These may provide opportunities to strengthen research through international collaboration or academic mobility. Applicants should consult Monash University for the detailed eligibility and funding arrangements associated with specific mobility schemes. Professional Development Opportunities PhD scholars will also have access to: Professional development training This may support the transition from doctoral research into academic, policy, industry or research careers. The programme is therefore intended not only to support thesis completion but also to strengthen participants’ broader research profiles. Industry Engagement Successful candidates may also access: Opportunities for industry engagement This feature is particularly relevant because AI governance and implementation increasingly involve collaboration between: Universities Technology companies Governments Regulators Civil society Creative industries Policy organizations Researchers interested in the practical impact of their work may therefore have opportunities to engage beyond academia. Interdisciplinary Supervision The scholarship call emphasizes: Interdisciplinary supervision AI-related societal questions rarely fit entirely within one academic discipline. For example, an investigation of algorithmic discrimination could potentially involve: Political science Sociology Law Policy studies Ethics Data governance Similarly, AI and creative labour might involve: Cultural studies Media studies Labour studies Sociology Music Creative practice Interdisciplinary supervision can therefore help doctoral candidates address these complex questions from multiple perspectives. Suggested Research Projects Monash Arts has identified several possible research topics associated with academics already working in these fields. Applicants are encouraged, where feasible, to align their proposals with these suggested projects. However, candidates should discuss their proposed research with the relevant prospective supervisor before submitting an application. 1. Co-designing AI Companionship to Promote Young People s Social Health and Wellbeing Proposed supervisor: Dr Claire Tanner This project focuses on: AI companionship and young people’s social health and wellbeing. The emergence of conversational AI and increasingly personalized AI systems raises important questions about how young people may interact emotionally or socially with technology. The project creates space for research into how AI companionship might be designed, understood or evaluated in relation to youth wellbeing. 2. Public Resistance to and Rejection of AI in Everyday Life Proposed supervisor: Professor Neil Selwyn Much discussion of technological innovation assumes that people will inevitably adopt new technologies. This project instead focuses on: Resistance to AI and: Rejection of AI in everyday life. It offers an opportunity to investigate why individuals or communities may choose not to adopt particular technologies and what those decisions reveal about: Trust Power Autonomy Social expectations Technology adoption 3. AI for Inclusive CALD Ageing and Care Communication Proposed supervisor: Dr Hui Huang This project considers AI in the context of ageing and communication involving culturally and linguistically diverse communities , often described using the abbreviation CALD. The research could contribute to questions surrounding: Inclusive communication Ageing Care Language Cultural diversity AI-mediated services 4. AI and the Future of Democratic Life: Participation, Persuasion and Public Trust Proposed supervisor: Dr Charles Crabtree This project addresses the relationship between: Artificial intelligence Democracy Political participation Persuasion Public trust AI increasingly influences how political information is produced, distributed and consumed. Research in this area may therefore have important implications for democratic institutions and governance. 5. From Generative AI to Generative Futures in Music Proposed supervisors: Dr Rod Davies and Dr Nicole Canham The full proposed theme is: From generative AI to generative futures in music: mapping future professionalism for evolving music labour markets. This research focuses on the impact of generative technologies on: Music Professional identities Creative labour Employment Future music industries It may appeal particularly to researchers working across creative practice, cultural policy, music studies and labour research. 6. Human Craft, AI and the Future of Screen Aesthetics Proposed supervisor: Dr Elliott Logan This project focuses on how artificial intelligence may affect: Human creative craft Screen production Visual aesthetics Creative processes The research offers an opportunity to investigate changing relationships between human creative practice and AI-supported or AI-generated media. 7. Human Labour and Automation in the Warehouse and Logistics Industry Proposed supervisor: Dr Christopher O Neill This project addresses the relationship between: Human labour Automation Warehousing Logistics AI and automation are transforming workplaces, particularly sectors characterized by data-driven monitoring and increasingly automated processes. The project could contribute to wider discussions surrounding the future of work. 8. Auditing Algorithms: Detecting and Reducing Discrimination in AI-Driven Decisions Proposed supervisor: Dr Charles Crabtree Algorithmic systems increasingly influence decisions affecting individuals and communities. This project focuses specifically on: Algorithm auditing Discrimination AI-driven decision-making The research has potentially significant implications for: Equality Governance Regulation Public policy Institutional accountability 9. The Changing Nature of Digital Inequalities in an Age of AI Proposed supervisor: Professor Neil Selwyn Digital inequality has traditionally concerned differences in: Technology access Connectivity Digital skills Digital participation AI introduces additional dimensions to these inequalities. This project investigates how digital disadvantage may change in an increasingly AI-dependent society. Can Applicants Propose Other AI Research Topics? The call provides suggested topics but describes applicants as researchers interested in addressing the contemporary and future challenges associated with artificial intelligence and digital transformation. Applications are expected to: Fit within the overall scope of the AI-focused scholarship call. Align, where feasible, with one of the proposed topics. Demonstrate an understanding of the proposed research area. Applicants should therefore discuss any alternative idea with a prospective Monash supervisor before assuming that it fits the scholarship. Who Should Apply? Monash Arts welcomes applicants from diverse backgrounds across: Humanities Social sciences Creative arts Candidates should be interested in social, cultural, political or environmental challenges associated with the rapid development of AI. Potential disciplinary backgrounds may therefore include: Sociology Political science International relations Public policy Philosophy Ethics Media studies Communication Cultural studies Anthropology Law Digital humanities Creative arts Music Labour studies Education Related HASS disciplines The exact academic background should align with the proposed PhD topic. Academic Requirements The selection committee will prioritize applicants holding an: Australian Honours degree or equivalent international qualification or: Master’s degree in a cognate discipline aligned with the proposed research project. The qualification should demonstrate: A significant research component. Candidates should therefore have previous experience undertaking substantial independent research. First-Class Honours / H1 Requirement Preference will be given to candidates who have achieved: First-Class Honours / H1 or equivalent This is an important indication of the competitiveness of the scholarships. The Faculty of Arts graduate research admissions process determines whether international qualifications meet the relevant standard. Significant Research Component Candidates should have completed a substantial research component as part of their previous qualification. Examples could include: Honours thesis Master’s dissertation Research thesis Substantial independent research project Applicants should make this research preparation clear in their CV and application documents. Full-Time Enrollment Is Mandatory Scholarship recipients must be enrolled: Full-time Part-time enrollment is not offered under the conditions stated in this call. On-Campus Attendance Is Mandatory Successful candidates must also study: On campus This means scholars should be prepared to live in or around Melbourne and undertake their research from the relevant Monash campus. International candidates should therefore consider: Australian student visa requirements Relocation costs Housing Living costs Health insurance Travel arrangements when preparing for potential study in Australia. Research Proposal Discussion Is Required Before Applying One of the most important application requirements is that candidates must: Discuss their research proposal with an aligned prospective supervisor before submitting the application. title: UN Junior Professional Officer (JPO) Programme 2026: Belgium-Funded Opportunities in Political Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Coordination
summary: The United Nations Junior Professional Officer (JPO) Programme offers young professionals an opportunity to gain practical experience working within United Nations organizations, funds, programmes and offices involved in development, humanitarian affairs, policy, coordination and other areas of international cooperation. In August 2026, Belgium announced three new JPO positions for young professionals seeking experience within the UN system. The available positions are based in New York, East Jerusalem and Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire , and cover political affairs, humanitarian affairs and UN coordination . The current openings are particularly relevant to qualified young professionals interested in international development, multilateral affairs, humanitarian action, UN reform, policy coordination and international cooperation. Application deadline for all three positions: September 18, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. EST (New York time). What Is the United Nations JPO Programme? The United Nations Junior Professional Officer Programme is a professional development initiative designed to give young experts practical experience within the UN system. JPOs work within participating UN organizations, funds, programmes and offices that finance, support or implement development and other international programmes. The programme is designed to combine professional experience, training and exposure to the work of the United Nations . A JPO is not simply placed in an administrative position. Depending on the assignment, the officer can contribute to activities such as: Programme development Policy analysis Programme formulation Programme implementation Monitoring Evaluation Coordination Research Strategic planning Humanitarian affairs Political affairs International development Multilateral cooperation JPOs receive guidance and training from senior UN staff and participate in the work of their assigned organization. This makes the programme particularly valuable for young professionals who want to build a long-term career in the United Nations, international development, humanitarian affairs, diplomacy, public policy or multilateral organizations . Belgium-Funded UN JPO Opportunities Open in 2026 The latest Belgian call includes three specific JPO assignments. These are: JPO in Political Affairs – Support to UN Reform JPO in Humanitarian Affairs JPO in Coordination Although all three positions fall under the broader JPO Programme, they have different responsibilities, locations and institutional environments. Applicants should therefore carefully review the individual vacancy notice before applying. 1. How the Belgian JPO Programme Works The Belgian JPO Programme is connected to Belgian Development Cooperation and provides young professionals with an opportunity to work within participating UN organizations. According to the programme information, JPO assignments are based either: In one of Belgium s partner countries for development cooperation; At the regional level; or At the headquarters of a participating UN organization. The design of JPO positions takes into account the strategic priorities of Belgian Development Cooperation . JPOs are also expected to receive professional training and supervision from senior staff. What Does a JPO Actually Do? A Junior Professional Officer can become involved in different stages of programme and policy work. The programme description specifically indicates that JPOs may participate in: Programme definition JPOs can contribute to identifying priorities and helping define programmes and interventions. Programme formulation They can support the development and formulation of programmes, projects and policy initiatives. Programme implementation JPOs can participate in putting programmes into practice and supporting implementation activities. Monitoring They can contribute to monitoring progress, outputs, activities and results. Evaluation JPOs may also participate in assessing whether programmes and interventions are achieving their intended objectives. This combination gives participants exposure to the full programme cycle , rather than limiting them to one isolated area of work. Why the UN JPO Programme Is a Valuable Career Opportunity For young professionals interested in international development and multilateral organizations, a JPO assignment can provide valuable professional exposure. 1. Work Alongside Experienced UN Professionals JPOs receive training and professional support from senior staff. Develop Programme Management Skills Because JPOs can participate in programme formulation, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, the programme can help participants develop practical skills across the project cycle. These skills are transferable to careers in: UN agencies International NGOs Development organizations Government institutions Multilateral organizations Research organizations Consulting Public policy 4. Build International Professional Networks Working in a UN environment can allow young professionals to interact with colleagues from different countries, professional backgrounds and UN entities. title: CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026: Two-Year Technology Policy Fellowship for Leading Academics and Researchers
summary: The Center for Democracy Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is now accepting applications from established academics and researchers interested in bringing their scholarly expertise into conversations about technology policy, digital rights, democracy, privacy, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, free expression, and the future of the internet. Based in Washington, D.C., with remote participation allowed, the program creates a bridge between academic research and real-world public-interest technology policy. Rather than separating academic scholarship from policy development, CDT s Non-Resident Fellows Program gives researchers an opportunity to engage directly with the organization s research and policy teams, contribute expertise to emerging technology debates, and strengthen the public-policy impact of their own research. Applications for the 2026 intake are open until September 18, 2026 . About the Center for Democracy Technology The Center for Democracy Technology (CDT) is an organization working at the intersection of technology, public policy, civil liberties, and individual rights. CDT works to strengthen individual rights and freedoms by defining, promoting, and influencing technology policy and the architecture of the internet that increasingly shapes everyday life. Its areas of focus encompass some of the most significant technology-policy questions facing governments, researchers, companies, civil society organizations, and communities today. These areas include: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Governance Cybersecurity and Standards Elections and Democracy Equity in Civic Technology Free Expression Government Surveillance Open Internet Privacy and Data Through its research, advocacy, policy engagement, and collaboration with experts, CDT seeks to ensure that technological development and technology policy protect people s rights and freedoms. What Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program? The CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is a two-year engagement designed to connect leading scholars and academics with CDT s technology-policy work. The program provides Fellows with opportunities to bring their research and specialist knowledge directly into CDT s policy conversations. Fellows can exchange ideas with CDT staff, participate in discussions surrounding emerging issues, and help inform how the organization approaches the social, political, economic, legal, and technical implications of rapidly developing technologies. CDT intentionally brings together Fellows from diverse academic disciplines, institutions, and areas of expertise. This interdisciplinary approach reflects the reality that technology policy is no longer confined to computer science or law. Technology influences virtually every aspect of modern society, meaning that understanding its effects requires perspectives from numerous disciplines. CDT therefore welcomes expertise spanning fields such as: Sociology Psychology Computer science Economics Communications Political science Human-computer interaction Media studies Law Other relevant interdisciplinary fields Through this diverse community, Fellows can help CDT understand the complex relationship between technology and the institutions, communities, governments, economies, and individuals affected by it. Bridging Academic Research and Technology Policy One of the central purposes of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is to help close the gap between academic research and public-interest technology policy . Academic researchers can produce significant evidence, theories, frameworks, and findings concerning emerging technologies. However, translating that research into policy discussions and practical public-interest outcomes can require connections between scholars and organizations directly involved in policy development. The Non-Resident Fellows Program creates opportunities for researchers and technology-policy practitioners to learn from each other. For academics, this can provide greater exposure to policy discussions and the opportunity to understand how research can contribute to practical debates. For CDT, Fellows provide access to expertise from leading researchers working across a broad range of disciplines. The program also places Fellows within a wider community of researchers and technology-policy experts, providing opportunities to establish relationships, exchange ideas, and potentially collaborate on some of the most important questions at the intersection of technology and democracy. Objectives of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program The program is designed for researchers who want to engage directly with and contribute to CDT s policy work. CDT Fellows volunteer their time to pursue three broad objectives: 1. Inform and Advance CDT s Research and Policy Work Fellows contribute academic knowledge, research findings, disciplinary expertise, and perspectives that can strengthen CDT s research and policy activities. Their involvement can help the organization consider technology-policy questions through different academic lenses and incorporate relevant scholarly evidence into its work. 2. Amplify CDT s Voice and Expand Its Expert Network Fellows can help connect CDT with leading academics and specialists working on relevant issues. These relationships can strengthen the exchange of information between academic communities and public-interest technology-policy practitioners. 3. Strengthen the Policy Impact of Fellows Research The relationship is intended to benefit Fellows as well. CDT aims to work with Fellows to strengthen the public engagement and policy impact of their academic research, potentially helping important scholarly work reach audiences involved in technology-policy conversations. Who Is CDT Looking For? CDT is seeking researchers from diverse experiences and backgrounds who are advocating for global digital rights . Applicants may come from a wide variety of disciplines. Relevant backgrounds include, but are not limited to: Sociology Psychology Computer science Economics Communication Political science Human-computer interaction Media studies Law The breadth of disciplines reflects CDT s recognition that digital rights and technology policy involve technical, legal, political, social, economic, cultural, and behavioral considerations. Minimum Qualifications for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program Applicants should carefully review the eligibility conditions because this opportunity is specifically targeted at established academics rather than students or early-stage postdoctoral researchers. Qualified applicants must be prepared to commit to a two-year non-resident engagement with CDT . Applicants must also: Hold a full-time position at an academic institution . Have published impactful work in peer-reviewed academic venues . Have experience working on technology-policy issues relevant to CDT s areas of work. Ideally possess a terminal degree, such as a Ph.D., J.D., or equivalent experience within their respective field. Have relevant expertise that can contribute meaningfully to CDT s research and policy activities. Be able to commit to the requirements of the two-year program. CDT places particular emphasis on candidates whose technology-policy experience relates to developments in the United States and European Union . Importantly, the program is not open to current students or postdoctoral researchers . What Will CDT Non-Resident Fellows Do? Non-Resident Fellows are expected to become active intellectual contributors to CDT s broader research and policy community. Their engagement can include participating in policy strategy calls and joining briefings concerning emerging technology-policy issues. Fellows are also encouraged to: Contribute original writing to the CDT blog. Present their research and expertise. Participate in collaborative projects with CDT s research and policy teams. Provide feedback on policy positions. Contribute perspectives on white papers. Provide feedback on research. Review or contribute to other relevant CDT outputs. These activities provide multiple ways for Fellows to translate academic expertise into practical policy engagement. Required Contribution During the Two-Year Fellowship In addition to committing to serve as a Non-Resident Fellow for at least two years, each Fellow agrees to complete at least one specified contribution during the two-year period . The contribution should concern issues relevant to CDT s work and be timely. A Fellow can satisfy this requirement by undertaking at least one of the following: Co-authoring a CDT blog post or participating in a CDT Tech Talk podcast; Speaking, presenting, or otherwise contributing to a CDT-branded event; or Collaborating with CDT on the development of a funding proposal. These requirements provide Fellows with flexibility to contribute in a way that aligns with their expertise and professional interests. Participation in CDT Events and Policy Discussions Fellows may also be invited to participate in CDT-branded events when appropriate. Examples can include: CDT Working Groups Policy roundtables Public events Webinars Other relevant CDT programs and discussions Fellows are additionally encouraged to promote CDT through their external professional and academic networks. This can involve sharing relevant CDT outputs, promoting job, internship, and externship opportunities, and connecting CDT with emerging research, policy conversations, events, or experts within Fellows academic institutions and professional networks. Opportunities for Collaborative Research The fellowship can extend beyond discussions and events into collaborative research. CDT Non-Resident Fellows may be invited to conduct research alongside CDT on mutually agreed projects connected to the organization s core research and advocacy priorities. Fellows may also proactively propose joint research projects they believe would complement CDT s work. However, applicants should understand that proposing a project does not necessarily mean it will automatically proceed. CDT evaluates proposed collaborations in the context of its: Organizational objectives Current priorities Available capacity Resources This provides room for innovative collaboration while ensuring projects remain aligned with CDT s broader mission and capabilities. Memorandum of Understanding for Selected Fellows Every Non-Resident Fellow will receive a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) at the beginning of their term. The MOU will establish important aspects of the two-year relationship between the Fellow and CDT. It will outline: Key dates during the fellowship; Expected deliverables for the two-year term; and Guidelines governing the appropriate use of CDT branding. This provides Fellows and CDT with a shared framework for expectations and engagement throughout the program. How CDT Supports Its Non-Resident Fellows The relationship between CDT and its Fellows is designed to involve active support and engagement rather than simply providing Fellows with a title. At the beginning of the program, CDT conducts an orientation program . The orientation includes information concerning: How Non-Resident Fellows work with CDT; How CDT promotes Fellows research; and How Fellows can participate in the technology-policy process. Following orientation, CDT commits to keeping Fellows connected with relevant developments and opportunities. Access to Technology and Internet Policy Insights CDT plans to provide Fellows with regular updates regarding important technology and internet-policy developments. Fellows may also be engaged in relevant working groups and can receive expert insights connected to their research interests. This exposure can be particularly valuable to academics seeking stronger connections between their research and ongoing policy discussions. Invitations to CDT Events and Programs Fellows become active members of CDT s wider community and can receive invitations to relevant events and programs throughout their participation. All Fellows are invited as CDT guests to certain public events and webinars, including the organization s Annual Dinner, Tech Prom . Fellows will also have opportunities to interact directly with CDT experts. At the same time, CDT welcomes Fellows feedback and recommendations, allowing academics to contribute their perspectives to the organization s work on developing trends and emerging technology-policy issues. Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program Remote? Yes. The opportunity is listed in Washington, District of Columbia, United States , but the position allows remote participation . This is consistent with the structure of the opportunity as a Non-Resident Fellows Program. Applicants should nevertheless carefully assess whether their professional position, expertise, and availability allow them to participate meaningfully in CDT s activities throughout the two-year engagement. Duration of the Program Selected applicants must commit to serving as CDT Non-Resident Fellows for at least two years . The two-year structure allows Fellows to establish meaningful relationships with CDT researchers and policy professionals rather than participating through a short-term engagement. The MOU provided at the beginning of the fellowship will establish the key dates and deliverables applicable to each Fellow s term. Application Requirements Applicants must prepare several important documents. The required application materials are: 1. Full Curriculum Vitae Applicants must provide a comprehensive CV demonstrating their academic background, professional appointments, publications, research experience, relevant policy engagement, and other qualifications. 2. Relevant Writing Sample Candidates must submit a writing sample relevant to the opportunity. Given CDT s emphasis on impactful academic work and technology-policy expertise, applicants should consider selecting a sample that effectively demonstrates their research capabilities and relevant subject-matter knowledge. 3. Cover Letter Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining: Their interest in becoming a CDT Non-Resident Fellow; Their relevant experience; Their qualifications for the opportunity; and Why their expertise is appropriate for the program. Applicants should ensure that their cover letter clearly communicates how their academic expertise intersects with technology policy and CDT s areas of work. Important Document Submission Requirement There is an important formatting requirement applicants should not overlook. The CV, writing sample, and cover letter must be compiled into one PDF or document for submission . Applicants should therefore not prepare these documents as unrelated individual uploads unless the application system specifically instructs otherwise. Combining everything into a single organized file before beginning the final submission process can help ensure compliance with CDT s stated application instructions. How to Apply for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 Interested researchers should complete the application through CDT s official recruitment system. A practical application process would involve: Review the fellowship requirements carefully. Confirm that you hold a full-time academic position. Assess whether your research experience relates meaningfully to CDT s technology-policy priorities. Update your full academic CV. Select a relevant and strong writing sample. Prepare a tailored cover letter explaining your interest, expertise, and qualifications. Compile the CV, writing sample, and cover letter into one PDF or document . Access the official CDT careers page and locate the Non-Resident Fellows Program opening. Select Apply for this position. Complete the required application information and submit the combined document before the deadline. Applicants with questions about the program or application process can contact CDT s research team at research@cdt.org . APPLY NOW Application Deadline The application deadline for the Center for Democracy Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is Friday, September 18, 2026 . Prospective applicants are encouraged to prepare their materials well before the closing date, particularly because the application requires a CV, relevant writing sample, and tailored cover letter compiled into one document. Why Researchers Should Consider the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program For academics whose work intersects with digital rights and technology policy, the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program provides an opportunity to move beyond traditional academic publication and participate in broader policy conversations. Several aspects distinguish the program. Direct Engagement With Technology Policy Fellows can participate in strategy calls, emerging-issue briefings, policy discussions, and other activities that bring academic expertise closer to practical technology-policy work. Greater Policy Impact for Academic Research Researchers often seek ways to ensure their scholarship reaches audiences beyond academic journals and conferences. Through CDT, Fellows can explore opportunities to strengthen the public engagement and policy relevance of their work. Interdisciplinary Collaboration Technology policy requires perspectives from numerous fields. Researchers can become part of a community spanning law, political science, sociology, economics, psychology, communications, computer science, human-computer interaction, media studies, and other disciplines. Opportunities to Publish and Present Fellows may contribute to CDT s blog, participate in Tech Talk, present at CDT events, and engage in other public-facing opportunities. Potential Research Collaboration Researchers may have opportunities to collaborate with CDT on mutually agreed research projects and can propose projects relevant to the organization s priorities. Access to a Wider Technology-Policy Community Participation connects Fellows with CDT experts and a broader network of researchers and technology-policy professionals. Diversity, Equity and Inclusion CDT states that it is an equal opportunity and inclusive employer and does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, gender, gender expression, age, national origin, disability, marital status, or sexual orientation. The organization specifically states that it believes diversity enables stronger and more impactful work. Women, people of color, disabled people, members of low-income communities, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and members of other marginalized communities are strongly encouraged to apply. Key Details at a Glance Program: Center for Democracy Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 Organization: Center for Democracy Technology (CDT) Listed Location: Washington, District of Columbia, United States Participation: Remote participation allowed Duration: At least two years Target Group: Established academics and researchers holding full-time positions at academic institutions Primary Focus: Technology policy, digital rights, academic research, and public-interest technology policy Required Documents: Full CV, relevant writing sample, and cover letter Submission Format: Required materials must be compiled into one PDF or document Application Deadline: September 18, 2026 Conclusion The Center for Democracy Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 provides established academics and researchers with an opportunity to connect rigorous scholarly research with real-world technology-policy discussions. As questions surrounding artificial intelligence, privacy, cybersecurity, online expression, surveillance, democracy, data governance, digital equity, and the open internet become increasingly important, interdisciplinary academic expertise has an important role to play in shaping informed public policy. Through its two-year Non-Resident Fellows Program, CDT aims to bring researchers directly into this environment. Researchers with impactful peer-reviewed work, relevant technology-policy experience, and a full-time position at an academic institution should consider preparing their application materials early.
